The Big Story 

Air Force Secretary confirms US deployed weapons in space

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed Monday that the U.S. military has deployed a weapon into space, marking the first time an American official has acknowledged that Washington has such a capability. 

© Matt Rourke, Associated Press

Meink did not provide many details about the weapon or when it was launched, but he stated that it will “make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”

“We are increasing readiness against existing threats and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said at the annual Air, Space and Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Md. 

 

Meink’s acknowledgement prompted a stern reaction from China. 

 

“China stands for peaceful use of the outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a warzone,” China’s Foreign Affairs Ministry said Tuesday. “We urge the U.S. to stop its military build-up in the outer space, and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions.” 

 

Russia weighed in as well, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying Moscow believes “space must be free of any weapon,” according to state media. 

 

“We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space,” Peskov said. 

 

“Is there any question . . . about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons,” Meink told reporters on Monday when asked about potential criticism from China and Russia.

data.title: Rogers set to skip Michigan Senate debate over outlet's 'favoritism' toward El-Sayed
data.description:
Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) will skip Tuesday night’s debate with opponent Abdul El-Sayed (D), citing the moderator’s alleged “favoritism” toward the Democrat.

Alyssa Brouillet, the Rogers campaign’s communications director, said in a statement that Michiganders “deserve to see their candidates engage in a healthy, fair debate — not one compromised by media bias.” 

She singled out moderator Roop Raj, a journalist with Detroit’s Fox affiliate. The Rogers campaign said the anchor’s “bias and favoritism” led the former congressman to skip the debate — slated for 7 p.m. EDT.

“Roop Raj has made his position clear, from praising Abdul as ‘brilliant,’ to being celebrated by Hasan Piker as ‘my GOAT,’ and bragging about his political stunts,” Brouillet added. “Mike looks forward to making his case to working families and to making Abdul answer to voters for the conman he is.”

Rogers and El-Sayed are battling in one of just seven Senate races the election handicapper Cook Political Report rates as a “Toss Up.” As of Monday, The Hill’s polling partner, Decision Desk HQ gave, gave El-Sayed a 66 percent chance of succeeding outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

Despite Rogers’s absence from Tuesday’s debate, the event will go on. El-Sayed will attend the debate next to an empty podium, according to Fox 2 Detroit.

Raj defended himself against the charges of favoritism from Rogers’s campaign, saying on Fox 2’s “Good Day Detroit” show, “Nothing we do at this station is trying to take a side.”

“We ask tough questions about Republicans and Democrats each and every night on our political talk show, ‘The Pulse.’ But as you can imagine, the narrative is the narrative. And for whatever reason, the Rogers camp did not want to do a debate with Fox 2,” Raj said.

The reporter admitted he praised El-Sayed as “brilliant” due to his background as a Rhodes Scholar but added that he sees both Senate candidates as “tremendous political athletes.”

El-Sayed, meanwhile, insinuated Rogers was “chicken” for skipping the debate. In a video he posted Tuesday to social platform X, the Democratic nominee said Florida — where Rogers owns a home — has some “fine chickens” who “don’t want to debate.”

data.title: Fetterman attended retreat with Fox News executives in Montana
data.description:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), who has been known to buck his party, went to a retreat featuring key figures at Fox News in Montana, according to a new report.

According to a Tuesday report from the Washington Examiner, the Pennsylvania senator went to a retreat alongside Fox News executives in Montana two months ago, being invited to the event by the owners of the network.

The retreat, which happened in mid-July, took place at the ranch of the Murdoch family, one of the most powerful families in the media industry, the Examiner reported. Lachlan Murdoch, one of the family members, is the CEO of the parent company of Fox News.

Fetterman, according to the Examiner, headlined a social media-focused panel alongside Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) during the retreat. Fetterman, alongside three other sources, told the Examiner of his presence at the retreat.

“I was invited to go there,” Fetterman said Tuesday, per the Examiner.

Fetterman, who has rubbed fellow Democrats the wrong way in recent years, on Tuesday again emphasized that he would not become a Republican in the wake of a video appearance at the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention.

When asked by a Capitol Hill reporter if there was a possibility he would cross the aisle, Fetterman seemed frustrated.

“I’m not going to be a Republican. Why can’t you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar,” he said. “My name is not on the ballot. Chill.”

Fetterman’s Democratic colleagues expressed discontent with him after a video he made introducing his fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) at the midterm convention.

The Pennsylvania Democrat has also recently gone after the left flank of his party, including democratic socialists and those who have voiced opposition to U.S. support of Israel.

The Hill has reached out to Fox News and Fetterman’s office for comment.

data.title: Senate votes to advance bill to regulate college sports, athlete compensation
data.description:
The Senate voted Tuesday to advance the Protect College Sport Act, which would create national rules for compensating college athletes, limit transfers and mid-season coaching moves and set a five-year window for athletic eligibility, among other reforms.

It would protect the NCAA, college athletics’ governing body, from anti-trust lawsuits, establish caps on revenue sharing and allow schools to have retention funds for star players.

The Senate voted 74-24 to advance the legislation, despite the opposition from the NAACP, the AFL-CIO and its Sports Council and the Congressional Black Caucus.

The legislation passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee with bipartisan support in June after months of negotiations between the Republican chairman, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), and the Democratic ranking member, Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.).

The legislation requires agents to register with a state before representing student athletes and caps their fees at 5 percent. It guarantees scholarships for ten years after eligibility so athletes can complete their degrees after their playing days and it requires Division I schools to provide medical coverage while athletes are participating in sports.

The Senate voted to advance the legislation over growing public concern about the excesses of college athletics’ current patchwork of compensation, eligibility and name, image and likeness rules.

LSU football coach Lane Kiffin caused an uproar when he considered adding players cut from the NFL to Tigers’ roster.

Dae’Quan Wright, a former Ole Miss tight end, practiced with LSU’s team after being waived by the Cleveland Browns, for example.

Another controversy erupted when quarterback Brendan Sorsby was ruled ineligible by the NCAA for sports gambling, including placing bets on his own team, after signing a lucrative name, image and likeness contract with Texas Tech.

“College sports today are in crisis,” Cruz said on the Senate floor before the vote.

“For years court decisions, litigation, conflicting state laws, unlimited transfers, eligibility issues and inconsistent enforcement has chipped away at the foundation of college athletics. The result is what we’re seeing right now, the Wild West,” he said.

Cantwell said that universities are borrowing millions of dollars and cutting women’s and Olympic sports to feed their football programs and “smaller schools have become unpaid development leagues for the giants.”

She noted that some college agents are now taking 20 percent to 25 percent of athletes’ NIL deals.

She also pointed out that the legislation would direct nearly $1 billion over the next six years to historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and has the support of the United Negro College Fund.

But some Democrats came out strongly against the bill, including Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), who played college football as a tight end at Stanford University.

“While a college student and player, I saw just how unjust the NCAA is. It’s a monopoly controlling $15 billion … and rapidly growing. The NCAA has a long record of ignoring the cries for justice from exploited college athletes,” he said.

He pointed out array of groups opposed to the bill, including the United College Athletes Association, the AFL-CIO, the NAACP and the Urban League.

“It is doing all kind of things to stop players from earning money, putting bureaucracy between them and the possibilities but it does nothing to affect coaches,” he said, noting that college coaches make some of the largest salaries in sports.

Cruz, the bill’s sponsor, however, argued that without congressional action, many schools would be forced to shutter their football programs or to end non-revenue-producing sports and women’s sports programs because of the strain of competing with bigger schools’ robust name, image and likeness compensation programs.

“We can sit on the sidelines and watch college sports continue to unravel or we can step on the field and lead,” he said, emphasizing that more than 370 universities have endorsed the bill.

“If the Senate doesn’t act, hundreds of thousands of those students will see their roster slots go away and their scholarships go away,” he said.

A group of college coaches, including Arkansas basketball coach John Calipari, visited Capitol Hill on Monday to promote the legislation.

Calipari told NewsNation in an interview that under current rules college coaches have stopped recruiting high school players to instead focus on recruiting older players, transfer players and European players.

“I got involved to say ‘This ain’t right for American kids,’” he said.

data.title: Democratic defectors rescue Republicans — again
data.description:
A pair of centrist Democrats crossed the aisle on Tuesday to help GOP leaders advance a number of bills, marking the second time this month that Democratic leaders have failed to unite their caucus against the Republicans’ messaging agenda. 

The defections frustrated their fellow Democrats and are sure to raise new questions about how leaders are managing their caucus, especially heading into elections where they’re hoping to flip control of the House. 

Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) joined Republicans to pass a procedural rule that allows a host of proposals — including a Russian sanctions bill opposed by Democrats — to come to the floor for final votes. 

The Democrats’ help was crucial in putting the rule over the top, because Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and his leadership team were wrestling with their own internal revolt in the form of conservatives who were threatening to oppose the measure. 

In the end, Johnson convinced several of those GOP holdouts to back the rule, which passed 214 to 211. Without Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, it would have failed 212 to 213. 

The defections are sure to outrage Democrats — leaders and rank-and-file members alike — who were up in arms earlier in the month after the same two Democrats helped Johnson pass a similar rule advancing a separate legislative package, which consisted mostly of GOP messaging bills designed to help Republicans keep the House in November’s midterms. 

On Tuesday evening, some of those internal frustrations were already trickling out. 

“It’s unfortunate, it doesn’t advance the work of the American people,” Rep. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) said after the vote. “That’s two individuals that are out of step with the American people that are within our party, and so hopefully there’s a wave of new people that are coming in that can overwhelm that margin.” 

After the first round of defections, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) had called a special meeting of the Democrats’ internal rules committee to discuss potential changes — and potential disciplinary measures — designed to keep the party united on procedural votes. Some Democrats wanted to strip Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez of their committee seats. 

That process fizzled with no disciplinary measures taken. (Jeffries huddled with Gluesenkamp Perez, who’s in a tough reelection contest, and said he was satisfied with the discussion. Golden is retiring). 

But the centrists’ decision to defect once again is sure to renew the conversation about how to keep lone-wolf members closer in line, especially on procedural votes. And it’s likely to raise questions about whether Democratic leaders didn’t draw a harder line the first time around. 

“You have to tell people. And that’s the big deal,” Rep. Juan Vargas (D-Calif.) said after the first episode. “It’s not how you vote, it’s that you tell people and be up front.”

Sudiksha Kochi contributed reporting.

data.title: Wicker, Shaheen to propose resolution urging U.S. cooperation with Russian pro-democracy movement
data.description:
A pair of influential bipartisan Senators plan to introduce a resolution Wednesday calling on the State Department to bolster cooperation with Russia’s pro-democracy movement inside and outside the country, according to a draft obtained exclusively by The Hill. 

Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) introduced the non-binding resolution to coincide with a major gathering of Russian dissidents in Washington D.C., called the Washington Dialogue.

It’s the second time the dialogue has convened, sponsored by the National Endowment for Democracy, the Congressionally-funded democracy promotion organization, and the Free Russia Foundation, founded by Russian dissidents, including those who have served time in Putin’s jails and been freed with U.S. intervention. 

The resolution condemns Russian President Vladimir Putin’s repression at home and the war against Ukraine, along with Russia’s detention of Americans, including Stephen Hubbard. He was captured by Russian forces after the invasion of Ukraine, accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Hubbard denies he is a soldier and he is designated by the U.S. as wrongfully detained. 

Wicker, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the resolution honored assassinated Russian political activists — specifically Boris Nemtsov, a prominent Putin critic who was killed in 2015 by gunmen with alleged links to the Russian government; and the prominent Putin opponent, Alexei Navalny. European governments blamed the Russian government for Navalny’s death by poison in 2024. 

“My colleague Senator Shaheen and I introduce this resolution for Nemtsov, for Navalny, and for the courageous Russians who carry their torch today,” Wicker said in a statement provided to The Hill. 

“Putin casts a repressive shadow over Russia, but these heroes work toward a bright future they cannot yet see. The U.S. Senate honors their efforts and looks forward to the day when Russia is led by and for its people.”

Shaheen, in a statement to The Hill, said the resolution aims to “champion those who fight for democracy within Russia and hold the Russian government accountable for the crimes it has committed against its own people.”

“Putin’s war of aggression against Ukraine was rooted in his fear that the Russian people would see Ukraine’s progress in creating a more democratic, prosperous country and want the same for their own country,” said Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. 

“Putin has used cruel tactics on his own people: suppressing dissent through brutal violence, proliferating state-sponsored repression and undermining democracy with election interference and through disinformation campaigns.” 

The resolution acknowledges that it is in the national interest of the U.S. to support democratic actors in Russia, commends the work of Russian civil society and independent media to expose and respond to crimes by Putin’s government and pursue accountability. 

The resolution comes ahead of Russian parliamentary elections taking place between September 18 and 20, the first to be held since Russia launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in Feb. 2022. 

Putin’s party, United Russia, is widely expected to sweep the election, although close attention will be paid to whether the party can get the more than 300 seats needed for a super-majority and push through constitutional changes without other parties’ support.

Russia’s Supreme Court has barred the liberal Yabloko party from the party-list ballot, the only registered party to oppose Russia’s war in Ukraine, while other opposition politicians have been banned from running,  Reuters reported. 

Putin, in power as president or prime minister since 2000, has consolidated his control over the country by cracking down on any political opposition and imposing strict censorship to stifle independent media, connections to international organizations or free access to the internet. 

There are an estimated 1,700 political prisoners in Russian jails, according to human rights monitors, and nearly one million Russians have left the country since Feb. 2022.

data.title: Benchmark bond yield reaches highest level in nearly 20 years
data.description:
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond reached its highest point since before the 2008 financial crisis on Tuesday, portending increased borrowing costs for millions of Americans. 

The 10-year Treasury bond yield peaked at 5.041 percent Tuesday morning, the note’s highest intraday mark since July 2007. The note closed at above 5 percent for the first time in 19-plus years. 

The 10-year bond yield tracks closely with the average 30-year mortgage rate, which reached a 14-month high of 6.76 percent last week. A rise in the 10-year bond yield could spell increases in auto and student loan interest rates.

Investors globally have fled the global bond market this summer, as mounting public debt and rising oil prices due to the Iran war create the perfect storm of economic uncertainty. The 10-year bond yield is more than a full percentage point above where it closed at the day before the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran conflict.

The longer-term 30-year Treasury bond yield, meanwhile, closed at nearly 5.37 percent on Tuesday. The 30-year bond yield is up roughly 74 basis points, each of which equate to 0.01 percent, from closing time the day before the Iran war began.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has sought to tamp down bond yields by increasing the amount of government bonds his department can repurchase, namely 10- to 20-year securities. The Treasury carried out that directive last Thursday, buying back nearly $5.2 billion worth of those longer-term bonds. 

The strategy has yet to pay off in the form of lower yields, but Bessent defended it on Tuesday. During an appearance before the House Financial Services, the Treasury Secretary said the Treasury has conducted its “two most successful” auctions in the last two decades since the policy change went into effect.

“The U.S. bond market, it continues, during [the] past month … since President Trump has come in, it has been the best-performing bond market in the developed world,” Bessent told Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.).

The 10-year bond yield hitting a 19-year high comes a day before the Federal Open Market Committee will decide whether to cut, hold or raise interest rates. Traders are pricing in a greater than 92 percent chance the central bank will raise rates by a quarter point, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

data.title: The Memo: Blanche blasts through norms as Rose Garden 'press secretary'
data.description:
An administration that often exhibits ostentatious pride in bursting through norms did so yet again on Tuesday afternoon, when Attorney General Todd Blanche took a turn as de facto White House press secretary.

Blanche spoke to reporters in the Rose Garden, mixing together commentary on legal matters, praise of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s prosecution of the Iran war, jabs at the Biden administration, an insistence that the United States had to win the artificial intelligence (AI) race, and even some careful comments about the recent wedding of Donald Trump Jr.

Blanche also took the time to poke fun at the assembled media — albeit with a demeanor that did not suggest any great mirth on his part.

“I notice you guys are sweating, which is nice. I love to see that,” he said just before taking questions.

“I’m very sorry that you’re sweating. I’m not really sorry,” he said near the end.

The mere fact that Blanche, a former personal lawyer to Trump, now serves as attorney general (AG) is exceptional in itself. The AG and the Department of Justice (DOJ) have traditionally been seen as without precise parallels elsewhere in government.

The DOJ and its leader have been expected to demonstrate some level of independence from the political wishes of the president they serve. Equally, past presidents have — for the most part — sought to avoid the appearance that they are pushing the DOJ in ways that would erode this perception.

The extent to which such niceties have been truly observed is debatable, to be sure. But it is hard to imagine a banner with the president’s face being unfurled from the DOJ’s Washington headquarters previously, as has been the case during this administration.

Trump, for his part, famously and publicly appealed to Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, to speed up prosecution of his enemies. He has at various times named other foes whom he believes should be targeted, only for prosecutors to follow through. 

This has led to some embarrassing outcomes — such as when a grand jury declined in February to return indictments against six Democratic lawmakers who had released a video urging U.S. troops not to obey illegal orders.

Trump had suggested their actions amounted to “seditious behavior.” The grand jurors didn’t even accept there was a case to answer.

Blanche’s appearance wasn’t even the first transgressive act of the day from within the administration. 

FBI Director Kash Patel had earlier been asked by lawmakers about the lifting of the bureau’s previous automatic ban on new trainees if they had been found to engage in prostitution or bestiality.

Less luridly, but more controversially, Trump had inveighed against the Supreme Court on social media earlier on Tuesday. His anger had been sparked by an adverse ruling the previous evening, in which the high court rejected Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting in time for the midterm elections.

Trump’s reaction was to complain that “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” and to further insist that “Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America.”

Trump also asserted, in jeering reference to the three justices he nominated during his first term: “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”

The court ruling came in sparse form on Monday evening, but Team Trump appeared to have lost 7-2, with none of his three nominees — Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh or Amy Coney Barrett — fully backing him.

Blanche, in the Rose Garden, cast the media storm that immediately followed Trump’s comments as much ado about nothing. He said the administration would “of course” follow the ruling, but continue its efforts to ensure a “fair election.”

“He is very frustrated,” the attorney general said of the President. “He has every right — and indeed he should — communicate his concerns with the Supreme Court whenever he has them.”

Later, Blanche was asked whether, during his time in private practice, he would have advised a client to take on a court in the manner of Trump’s blasts at the Supreme Court. The attorney general rejected the comparison.

“He’s the President of the United States, so the real question is whether the President of the United States is allowed to be critical of another branch of government,” Blanche said. “And the answer to that is: Absolutely, of course he is.”

At times, the attorney general was more circumspect. He largely evaded a question about whether he asked for the resignation of Joe DiGenova, a fervently pro-Trump figure and former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia who had been investigating whether there was a “conspiracy” against Trump during previous Democratic administrations.

A separate question about a seeming lack of action following the FBI’s controversial raid on a Fulton County, Ga., election hub in January also elicited little real information.

Still, he was not always so cautious. He alleged that, in a previous incarnation, the FBI had sought to “put [Trump] in prison till he dies.”

Pressed on questions around the ethics of a Russian oligarch paying for some of the wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr. and his new wife Bettina in May, Blanche shot back to a reporter: “When you say, ‘Am I investigating’ — am I investigating what? And when you say this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know if that’s true or not.”

The person in question, Umar Kremlev, had been bestowed a state honor by Putin, according to investigative website ProPublica, which broke the story.

Elsewhere, the nation’s chief law enforcement officer provided praise for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who he said was doing a “phenomenal job”; and for former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who Blanche praised for her handling of the job he was trying to fill, at least for about 35 minutes.

“She’s a lot better than me,” the attorney general said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: House Oversight votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein deposition
data.description:
The House Oversight Committee on Tuesday in a unanimous bipartisan vote held Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he failed to appear for the deposition related to his ties to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Lawmakers have sought to question Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management, about payments he made to Epstein totaling millions over a number of years. The investor says the payments were for tax and estate planning, among other services, and he had no knowledge of any abuse.

Black walked out of a voluntary interview with the panel two months ago, and he sued the committee earlier this month on the day he was commanded to appear for a deposition.

“Mr. Black is hiding behind litigation to delay having to provide answers to the American people. No one is above the law. Mr. Black will be treated the same as anyone else in this investigation, and his actions have consequences. A little over two months ago, Mr. Black appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview, but only an hour into the interview, he began refusing to answer questions,” Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) said at the start of the hearing.

“Subpoenas are not suggestions; they carry the force of law and require full compliance.”

Comer said in addition to failing to comply with the subpoena for a deposition, Black also only supplied one nondisclosure agreement following a subpoena for documents, despite an indication from his attorneys that there were additional documents.

Ranking member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said the panel had numerous questions about Black’s financial ties to Epstein.

“We believe that Leon Black is at the heart of the Epstein network. This is a private equity billionaire worth roughly $13 billion dollars. We need to know why Jeffrey Epstein got over 180 million dollars from Mr. Black. We know this money enabled Epstein’s activities for years, and we need to know how and if it led to the abuse of women and girls. We need to know about Leon Black and Jeffrey Epstein’s financial dealings,” he said during the business meeting.

Black’s legal team did not immediately respond to request for comment.

His lawsuit, however, argues the committee lacks legal authority to enforce the subpoenas and that they improperly seek private information. 

“Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the complaint states. 

A contempt resolution must be brought to the full House floor for consideration. If it is approved, it acts as a referral to the Justice Department, which must then determine whether to press charges.

The vote was the latest example of bipartisanship when it comes to investigating the dealings of Jeffrey Epstein.

The House voted earlier this year to force the Justice Department to release files related to the deceased financier while the committee has requested to speak with or compelled interviews from numerous subjects.

In July, Comer said he would also like to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche.

data.title: Comey asks to push trial in seashell case to February
data.description:
Former FBI Director James Comey on Tuesday asked that his trial on charges of threatening President Trump’s life with seashells styled to spell “86 47” be moved to February.

Comey had previously motioned to have the trial start Oct. 21. His latest motion, written by defense attorney Joseph Zeszotarski Jr., requested that the date be moved “because additional time is needed to prepare for trial,” according to court documents.

Zeszotarski added that this includes time to prepare for any pretrial hearings, review discovery material and to consider and draft “various motions in limine.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) secured a second indictment against Comey in April in connection with a since-deleted Instagram post featuring the seashells in the sands of a North Carolina beach. The indictment claimed that the photo was a “serious expression of an intent to do harm” to Trump.

Comey has denied all wrongdoing, with his defense team previously arguing that “’86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”

Restaurant employees frequently use the term “86” when an item is unavailable or needs to be removed. The Merriam-Webster dictionary states that “86” originated from 1930s soda-counter slang indicating that an item was sold out.

The former FBI director’s legal team said in his motion to toss the case in July that their client was being targeted for exercising his First Amendment right by “publishing another person’s statement of political opposition.” They also argued that there is no definition of “86,” as seen in a dictionary, meaning “to kill.”

The DOJ discouraged the judge from tossing the case, stating that the photo of the seashells constituted a “true threat” to the president. Prosecutors argued that Comey acknowledged that some may have construed his post as a threat when he deleted it.

Comey wrote that he deleted the post after he “assumed” the shells were arranged in a “political message” and that he did not “realize some folks associate those numbers with violence,” leading him to delete the post, according to a May 2025 Instagram post.

Trump accused Comey of knowing what the message intended, telling Fox News’s Bret Baier in May 2025 that it “meant assassination.”

Comey is a longtime foe of the president and has publicly criticized Trump in the past. The president fired him FBI director in 2017 and the former FBI head later backed former Vice President Kamala Harris’s presidential bid in 2024 and former President Biden’s bid in 2020.
